reading.body:
The canonical visual explainers of how neural networks and transformers work are free, archived, and collectively maintained by academic communities rather than companies, making the core knowledge of AI architecture durable and widely accessible.

This collection spans five categories: peer-reviewed interactive articles, authored deep-dives, editable diagram libraries, live-code visualizations, and community wikis. Together they form a public substrate for learning what transformers do and how to communicate it. None require payment or corporate login. Most are version-controlled or archived, which means they persist even if original authors move on.

For AI specifically, this matters because the rate at which researchers and engineers can build scales with how quickly they can grasp and modify existing architecture. Visual explanations compress what would take weeks to derive from papers alone. The Illustrated Transformer appears in university courses worldwide not because it is mandated but because it is the fastest way to move from equations to intuition. When that knowledge lives in open repositories and browser-based demos, the cost of onboarding talent into AI work drops for any organization, anywhere.

What this data does not cover: implementation libraries, code frameworks, the quality or accuracy of specific explainers, or whether these resources reach the populations that most need them. It shows that free visual knowledge of AI exists and persists. It does not measure whether that knowledge translates into capability or opportunity at scale.
